newsitem.title: USA: State Department archive search for Nazi gold data.
newsitem.headline: State Department archive search for Nazi gold data.

text.p: Responding to calls from congressmen and Jewish activists, the U.S. government said on Friday it would scour its archives for information on what happened to gold and other assets looted by the Nazis.

The State Department promised a "thorough and immediate study" of what the U.S. government at the time knew about the disbursement of Nazi assets after the Second World War and the extent of U.S. contacts with the Swiss government on the question.

The Nazis deposited vast amounts of valuables taken from Holocaust victims in Swiss banks. The State Department move comes amid a growing dispute over whether the Swiss subsequently handed over all the assets.
A $20 billion class action suit was filed on Thursday in New York on behalf of Holocaust survivors against Swiss banks for allegedly refusing to return victims' money, jewelry and other valuables.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the study of U.S. archives, to be carried out by the department's Office of the Historian under chief historian Bill Slaney, would last two to three months and its results would be made public.

Republican Senator Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, last month called for the State Department to investigate what he called "50 years of deception" by Switzerland over the amount of funds deposited by the Nazis.

Burns said his department was responding to requests by D'Amato and the World Jewish Congress about "what the U.S. government knew about the disposition of Nazi assets at that time (and) whether or not we had diplomatic contact with the Swiss government."

He said there were unanswered questions about the roles of the U.S. and Swiss governments and the interaction between them. The State Department was treating this as a "highly urgent and priority matter."

"There have been enough serious calls for a review of U.S. actions during the period that the administration thought it was wise to undertake our own study, so that we could assure ourselves of all the facts," Burns told a news briefing.
In a statement of reaction, D'Amato said he welcomed the State Department's "finally waking up to this tragedy" but called it unfortunate that the department had taken "so many years" to do so.
"We are going to continue to pursue the facts, so we can get at the truth," he said. "We need to find how much money the Holocaust victims and their families are entitled to."

D'Amato has urged the United States to reopen negotiations with the Swiss on a treaty in which Switzerland agreed to give the Allies $60 million in compensation for accepting gold looted by the Nazis. He says archive documents show that the Swiss had up to $600 million in Nazi gold.
D'Amato on Wednesday sought information on the gold in letters to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Brussels-based Tripartite Commission for the Restitution of Monetary Gold.
He asked the Commission how much gold it had sent to the New York Fed, the Bank of England and other central banks since it was created in 1946 to resolve the issue of assets stolen by the Nazis.
Burns said it was "just too early to tell" whether Washington would seek to reopen negotiations with Switzerland.
A senior U.S. official said the new study would focus on such questions as "Did we do the right things, are there things we knew then that have not come to light since then?"
He said Washington had already spoken to the Swiss authorities about the study but that any further action after its publication "depends on what we find."

"Obviously we're going to want to discuss the contents of our findings with the Swiss government and with the world Jewish community and with the interested people who brought this forward to us," the official said.
